clue.text: Say this'll make you happy to be put in the picture

definitions.text: Say this'll make you happy to be put in the picture

parts.words: Say this'll make you happy to be put in the picture
parts.note: the word a photographer asks a sitter to say so that the mouth forms a smile for the photograph

explanation.surface: Someone is being promised happiness on being let in on the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in the picture' looks like the idiom for being informed; here it means being photographed.
explanation.definitionFit: Photographers traditionally ask their subjects to say this dairy word because it shapes the lips into a grin.

clue.text: Unfeeling dandy acted deliberately in this

parts.note: cold means unfeeling, without warmth
a blood is an old word for a fashionable young man about town

explanation.surface: A heartless fop behaved with intent.
explanation.walkthrough: A blood was a Regency-era rake or dandy. Someone who acts deliberately and without passion is said to do it in cold blood.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'in cold blood' describes doing something calmly and with premeditation, not in passion.

clue.text: Reversion to crown points to a swindle

parts.note: E and S are the compass points east and south
a cheat is a fraud or swindle

explanation.surface: Getting back to the throne involves a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: In old English law, land with no heir passed back to the Crown or lord by this process.
explanation.definitionFit: A feudal right by which the property of someone dying without heirs passes back to the state.

clue.text: Plant for delivering bundles?

parts.note: bundles are babies, which nursery legend says a long-legged bird brings, carried in its beak

explanation.surface: A factory set up to dispatch parcels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a factory and 'bundles' like parcels; it is a flower named after the beak of the bird said to deliver babies.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild flower of the geranium family whose long beaked fruit resembles the bill of the baby-bringing bird.

clue.text: His suit was made to last a dickens of a time

definitions.text: His suit was made to last a dickens of a time

parts.words: His suit was made to last a dickens of a time
parts.note: suit is a lawsuit, and 'a dickens of a time' points to Charles Dickens, whose novel has a Chancery case dragging on for generations

explanation.surface: A tailor boasts of a suit that wore well for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: The suit is not clothing but the endless Chancery lawsuit of Bleak House; 'dickens of a time' is an old phrase for a very long time, here naming the author too.
explanation.definitionFit: The family name in the interminable Chancery case of Dickens's novel, the suit that ate up its estate in legal costs.

clue.text: Burns to control flight in this environment

definitions.text: Burns to control flight in this environment

parts.words: Burns to control flight in this environment
parts.note: burns are rocket-engine firings that steer a craft, in the region of air and outer space beyond

explanation.surface: Fires are lit to keep an escape in check somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burns' are brief firings of a rocket motor, used to adjust a spacecraft's course.
explanation.definitionFit: The combined realm of the earth's atmosphere and outer space, in which aircraft and rockets operate.

clue.text: With this record, 26 is not without love

annotationWithheld.why: With this record, 26 is not without love: NOTE is record, but no reading of '26 (TENT) is not without love' builds the letters; the wordplay cannot be recovered
annotationWithheld.clue: With this record, 26 is not without love

clue.text: Old partisan concocted one story about the king

indicators.note: about means going round, so the shuffled letters surround the royal abbreviation
concocted means made up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A partisan of old made up a tale concerning the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concocted' shuffles I and STORY to YORIST, and 'about' puts K inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A supporter of the House of York in the fifteenth-century Wars of the Roses.

clue.text: Racecourse records, with order of merit

parts.note: EPs are extended-play records
OM stands for the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: A track's history is recorded alongside an honour.
explanation.walkthrough: The racecourse in Surrey that hosts the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: The Surrey downland course where the Derby and the Oaks are run.

clue.text: Unmanned Turk

annotationWithheld.why: Unmanned Turk: OTTOMAN less MAN gives the letters, but no clue word is left to define the answer; 'Unmanned' and 'Turk' are both wordplay

clue.text: With which employers strike back?

parts.note: a strike is normally a weapon of workers; this is the reverse measure, the employer shutting the workforce out

explanation.surface: Bosses look for a way to retaliate against their staff.
explanation.definitionFit: An employer's shutting of the workplace against staff in a dispute is the management counterpart of a strike.

clue.text: Vessels make sharp replies

definitions.meaning: glass flasks with long bent necks used in distilling

explanation.surface: Containers somehow answer back tartly.
explanation.definitionFit: A distilling flask with a bent neck shares its name with the verb for answering back with quick wit.

clue.text: Where 4 was brought to book

parts.note: 4 is the lawsuit from 4-across; 'brought to book' usually means made to answer for something, here literally put into a novel

explanation.surface: A culprit is finally made to account for himself somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought to book' wants to mean punished; here it means written into a book, the Dickens novel containing the case at 4-across.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dickens novel of 1853 in which the Chancery case of 4-across is the central plot.

clue.text: Bill in Ireland gets letters returned

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word for the letters is read backwards

parts.note: letters delivered by the post are mail

explanation.surface: An Irish parliamentary bill comes back with correspondence attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like legislation; it is a pet form of William, whose Irish form this is. 'returned' turns MAIL backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish short form of William, just as Bill is the English nickname for that same name.

clue.text: Helpful advances on one personal book

parts.note: subs are advance payments of wages
I is the Roman numeral one
a diary is a private record book

explanation.surface: Advances are made on the strength of a private journal.
explanation.walkthrough: SUBS is informal British for an advance on wages.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that serves in a supporting or auxiliary role gives assistance.

clue.text: Club beer for old 'Tories

parts.note: names both a club of Tory backbenchers in Queen Anne's reign and the strong ale brewed in the autumn month that they toasted

explanation.surface: A drinks list names the ale served to elderly Conservatives at their club.
explanation.walkthrough: The October Club was a group of high Tory MPs around 1710, named after the strong October ale they drank.
explanation.definitionFit: The tenth month gave its name to a strong autumn-brewed ale and to an early eighteenth-century Tory club.

clue.text: Top broadcaster is signally remote

parts.note: reads as a famous presenter, but means a distant body in space that sends out signals on radio waves

explanation.surface: A leading broadcaster is remarkably aloof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Signally' looks like 'remarkably'; it means by sending signals. The answer is both a celebrity on the wireless and an astronomical radio source.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebrity of the wireless, and also an old name for a celestial object emitting strong radio waves.

clue.text: Was next to Mark East in the year of grace

indicators.note: in places the target and compass point inside the abbreviation for the Christian era

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, the year of our Lord
a butt is a target or mark to shoot at
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Someone stood beside Mark East in a year of the Lord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark East' reads like a person's name; it is BUTT (a target) and E, inside AD.
explanation.definitionFit: To border on something is to be adjacent to it, touching at the edge.

clue.text: Scott's Dr Jonas needing drink?

definitions.meaning: the fictional antiquary to whom Walter Scott addressed prefaces in several novels

explanation.surface: A Scott character is thirsty.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's Dr Jonas Dryasdust became a byword for a dull pedant; the phrase also means very parched.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's tedious antiquarian doctor, and a phrase for being utterly parched.

clue.text: How Cleopatra's pretty barge boys smiled!

definitions.text: How Cleopatra's pretty barge boys smiled!

parts.words: How Cleopatra's pretty barge boys smiled!
parts.note: recalls Enobarbus's description in Antony and Cleopatra of the pretty boys standing beside her on the barge, like smiling Cupids

explanation.surface: An exclamation at the charming smiles of the boys on Cleopatra's barge.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's line runs 'On each side her stood pretty dimpled boys, like smiling Cupids'.
explanation.definitionFit: Small hollows appear in the cheeks of a smiling face, and Shakespeare uses this word for Cleopatra's attendant boys.

clue.text: Ragtime medley ? Get away!

indicators.note: a medley is a mixture, so the letters of the word are jumbled

explanation.surface: A pianist plays a ragtime medley and is told to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get away!' looks like an exclamation of disbelief; it is the verb meaning to move to another place.
explanation.definitionFit: To move from one region to another, as birds do seasonally.

clue.text: " What pipes and timbrels ? What wild —?"(Keats)

definitions.text: " What pipes and timbrels ? What wild —?"(Keats)

parts.words: " What pipes and timbrels ? What wild —?"(Keats)
parts.note: the missing last word of a line from Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn, describing the frenzied revellers on the urn

explanation.surface: A quotation from Keats with its final word left blank.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats ends the first stanza of his Grecian Urn ode with this word for wild rapture.

clue.text: A river wild cherry — far out of this world

parts.note: the Po is Italy's longest river
the gean is the wild cherry tree

explanation.surface: A wild cherry by a river is unearthly.
explanation.walkthrough: GEAN is a dialect word for the wild cherry. 'Out of this world' sounds like praise; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the point of an orbit farthest from the earth.

clue.text: Six leave Spanish port

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: Half a dozen people depart from a harbour in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A major Atlantic seaport in Galicia, north-west Spain.

clue.text: Sacred books could be saved

indicators.note: could be means the letters of the word may be turned into another arrangement

explanation.surface: Holy texts could be rescued.
explanation.definitionFit: The oldest scriptures of Hinduism, written in Sanskrit.

clue.text: Roomy enough but for a firm with two thousand hateful

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm
M is a thousand in Roman numerals, so two of them make MM
odious means hateful

explanation.surface: A space would be fine except that the company with two thousand staff is loathsome.
explanation.definitionFit: Spacious and comfortable, with plenty of room for its purpose.

clue.text: What geography is about, said E. C. Bentley

definitions.text: What geography is about, said E. C. Bentley

parts.words: What geography is about, said E. C. Bentley
parts.note: Bentley, inventor of the clerihew, wrote that geography was about these, while biography was about chaps

explanation.surface: A writer gives his view of the subject of geography.
explanation.walkthrough: E. C. Bentley's clerihew runs: 'Geography is about Maps, But Biography is about Chaps.'
explanation.definitionFit: Charts of the earth's surface, the core of geography according to Bentley's comic verse.

clue.text: Wine for a pitcher

definitions.meaning: a deep red Spanish wine, once used as communion wine

explanation.surface: Wine is offered to a baseball pitcher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitcher' looks like a jug or a thrower; it is someone pitching camp.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark red Spanish wine, and a canvas shelter that one pitches.

clue.text: In India lecturers allow for language variation

indicators.note: In tells us the answer sits inside the run of letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Indian academics make allowances for differences in how English is spoken.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the end of India and the start of lecturers.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional or social form of a language, differing in words, grammar and pronunciation.

clue.text: Tea with Paul arranged in a high flat

indicators.note: arranged means the letters of these words are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: Paul has tea laid out for him in his upper-storey apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High flat' looks like an apartment; it is raised level ground. 'arranged' shuffles TEA and PAUL.
explanation.definitionFit: An elevated stretch of land with a level top, a tableland.

clue.text: Automatic rises for the loud-mouthed?

parts.note: the Sten was a British automatic submachine gun of the Second World War
tors are rocky hills or rises, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Automatic pay increases are given to noisy people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Automatic rises' reads like pay rises that come without asking; it is a Sten gun plus tors, the rocky hilltops of south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Named after the loud-voiced herald in the Iliad, these are people with very powerful voices.

clue.text: It's much too early for this bird's song

definitions.text: It's much too early for this bird's song

parts.words: It's much too early for this bird's song
parts.note: a swan is said to sing only as it dies, so a young one is far from its final song

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the dawn chorus has started too soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too early' suggests dawn; it means too young for a swan song, the legendary song a swan sings before death.
explanation.definitionFit: A young swan, which by legend will sing only once, at its death, many years away.
